extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of Regency romance; general encyclopedia audience
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating or evaluating Regency romance novels—stories set in the British Regency/early 19th century with particular plot, stylistic, and historical conventions. Covers distinctions between Traditional Regencies and Regency Historical works and lists common plot elements and stylistic expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period setting (British Regency / early 19th century)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regency romances are set during the period of the British Regency (1811–1820) or the early 19th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the historical time through setting, social season events, manners, vocabulary and other period detail to place the story firmly in the Regency era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct genre conventions (plot and stylistic conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regency romances are a distinct genre with their plot and stylistic conventions, not merely contemporary romances transported to a historical setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the genre's recognizable structural and stylistic patterns (focus on social maneuvering, manners, formality of courtship, etc.) rather than only changing surface historical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and tonal model: Georgette Heyer / Novel of Manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventions derive not so much from 19th-century Austen but rather from Georgette Heyer and the fiction genre known as the Novel of Manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Heyer's approach to voice, social observation, pacing and witty morality as a model when aiming for a 'traditional' Regency tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional Regency: emphasis on the primary romance plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Works in the tradition of Georgette Heyer, with an emphasis on the primary romance plot, are considered Traditional Regency romances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the central narrative focused on the romantic relationship; secondary plots should support rather than overshadow the primary romance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical detail and voice replication (Traditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Regency Romance writers usually pay close attention to historical detail, as their readers are notorious for noting errors, and the writers often do extensive research so they can clearly understand and replicate the voice of the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thorough research and emulate period-appropriate diction, social protocols and manners; factual errors are especially noticed by fans of the subgenre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue-driven prose (intelligent, fast-paced dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: More traditional Regencies feature a great deal of intelligent, fast-paced dialogue between the protagonists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor lively exchanges and repartee to reveal character and advance the courtship; dialogue often carries much of the novel's wit and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of sexual explicitness (Traditional vs. Regency Historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Regencies typically contain very little explicit sex or discussion of sex, whereas Regency Historical (sensual Regency) novels are much more explicit and include many more love scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose explicitness consistent with subgenre expectations: minimal sexual content for Traditionals; more explicit love scenes for Regency Historicals seeking sensual appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regency Historical: social realism or modernized characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Regency Historical works may include more social realism, or conversely, anachronistically modern characterization—signifying setting in Regency England but plot, characterization, or prose style that extends beyond Heyer-like formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a Regency Historical, allow for modern sensibilities or realistic social issues in character behavior and themes, but be aware this moves away from the traditional formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depictions of the ton and social season activities
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the ton (le bon ton) and depictions of social activities during the social season—carriage rides, morning calls, dinner parties, routs, plays, operas, assemblies, balls, etc.—are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these social events as settings for character interaction, gossip, display of manners, and plot development; they help build the world and social stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to athletic pursuits of fashionable young men
rubrics_metrics.description: References to, or descriptions of, athletic activities engaged in by fashionable young men of the period, including riding, driving, boxing, fencing, hunting, shooting, etc., are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include period-appropriate pastimes to characterize gentlemen and signal class and leisure; such scenes can reveal personality and social status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in social class
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in social class are a common element of Regency romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class distinctions to create obstacles, tensions, mismatched expectations and negotiations around marriage and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriages of convenience and economic motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriages of convenience: a marriage based on love was rarely an option for most women in the British Regency, as securing a steady and sufficient income was the first consideration for both the woman and her family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray courtship and marital decisions within economic and social constraints of the period; marriage can be plot-driven by financial necessity rather than romance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: False engagements as a plot device
rubrics_metrics.description: False engagements appear as a recurring plot element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use false engagements (misunderstood or contrived betrothals) to create dramatic irony, obstacles to love, or social scandal that must be resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of courtesans/demireps/mistresses (cyprians, demireps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyprians (sex workers), demireps (women of ill repute), mistresses and other women employed by rakehell and men from the upper classes appear in the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate such figures to illustrate the period's sexual economy and social hypocrisies; they can create conflict, moral tension or contrast with heroine's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaken identity (deliberate or otherwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaken identity, deliberate or otherwise, is a common element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mistaken identity to generate misunderstandings, comic situations, or obstacles that test relationships and social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery or farce elements blended into plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery or farce elements are often present in Regency romance plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend comedic misunderstanding, farcical scenarios or light mystery to vary tone and create plot momentum beyond the central courtship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of peerage rank and the 'marriage mart' (titles matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rank system of the peerage of England plays a large role in the 'marriage mart' of Regency Romance; observers have noted a historically inaccurate and statistically unlikely overabundance of Dukes in the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use titles and rank to structure social ambitions and constraints, but be aware of realism vs. genre convention (the frequent appearance of high ranks like dukes is a trope rather than a demographic reality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of social ills and troubled protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors depict the underbelly of Regency society, exploring a variety of social ills; some feature seriously troubled heroes and heroines who suffer from post-battle trauma, alcoholism, depression, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for depth or social realism, portray psychological trauma and societal problems sensitively and realistically, integrating them into character arcs rather than treating them as mere plot devices.
